analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling along the Atlantic coast and Florida straits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee from May 2021 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a permanent ban into law against oil and gas drilling on the outer Continental Shelf in four areas: the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, and the Straits of Florida. It would bar the Interior Department from issuing any lease or authorization for exploration, development, or production there, including for gas and other minerals [S2] [S3]. Supporters frame this as protecting coastal economies and waters from spills; the drilling industry loses access to those waters. The bill never received a hearing or a vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023 [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities, tourism businesses, and commercial fisheries along the Atlantic and Florida coasts, who would be spared the risk of offshore spills; also beachgoers and coastal residents generally.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal towns, tourism, and fishing industries

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Interior Department from issuing any lease or authorization for exploration, development, or production of oil, gas, or other minerals in the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, and Straits of Florida planning areas [S2] [S3].
Makes the protection permanent by amending the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, so it cannot be undone by a future administration's leasing plan the way a policy memorandum can be [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose the chance to drill in Atlantic waters, and the federal government forgoes potential leasing revenue from those areas.

drawbacks.text: Restricting drilling in Atlantic waters removes potential domestic oil and gas supply, which critics argue can raise reliance on imports and do little to lower consumer energy prices; the affected areas are estimated to hold significant undiscovered reserves under general knowledge of federal OCS assessments.

A permanent statutory ban removes flexibility: if a future crisis made domestic production urgent, Congress would have to pass new legislation to reopen the areas, rather than an administration adjusting a leasing plan.
The federal government and Gulf-adjacent states forgo potential leasing revenue and shared royalties that Atlantic sales would have generated under the existing offshore revenue-sharing system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Atlantic and Florida coastal communities, the protection from spill risk to tourism, fishing, and shorelines is substantial and the cost — forgone drilling revenue and some added reliance on drilling elsewhere — falls mostly outside the region. The main honest objection is national: the bill narrows domestic energy supply at a time of price volatility, and a permanent ban is a blunt instrument compared with leasing restrictions that could be revisited.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2023 [S5].

narrative.text: Menendez introduced the bill on May 26, 2021; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day [S5] [S1].
No further action is recorded — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the 117th Congress [S5].
The bill drew 15 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents, and no Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies keep any future possibility of Atlantic leasing, and coastal communities remain exposed to whatever a future administration's leasing plan allows.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas drillers; coastal towns left exposed

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban Atlantic offshore drilling and referred it to committee [S1] [S5].

for.name: 14 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did [S4].

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Joe Manchin
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat without action until the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-led opposition to drilling bans meant it had no path to floor time.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Senate Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced to a vote where positions would have been recorded [S4].

industries.industry: Offshore oil and gas drilling companies
industries.note: The bill closes Atlantic and Florida-strait waters to new leasing and drilling, removing a source of future reserves and revenue. Keeping those waters open allows the industry to profit while coastal communities bear the spill risk, so its interest runs against the bill's beneficiaries.

industries.industry: Atlantic coastal tourism and commercial fishing
industries.note: A drilling ban protects beaches, fisheries, and coastal economies from the damage a spill would cause. These industries' fortunes rise and fall with the health of the same waters the public uses.

industries.industry: Gulf of Mexico and other OCS drillers
industries.note: The bill only covers Atlantic and Florida-strait planning areas, so Gulf and Pacific drilling operations are untouched. Restricting supply elsewhere can support prices for remaining producers.
